introduction: On this Sunday, the Book of Wisdom asks, Who can know God's counsel, unless God gives wisdom and sends his Holy Spirit? In the Gospel, Jesus tells the great crowds following him that discipleship has a cost; like someone building a tower, we must count the cost and be ready to put him first. Paul asks Philemon to welcome back the slave Onesimus as a beloved brother. Let us follow Christ with our whole hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, teach us to number our days, that we may gain wisdom of heart. Let us bring our prayers to the Lord.
intentions: For the Church: that she may follow Christ wholeheartedly and carry the cross with him. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who are enslaved or exploited: that they may be set free and treated as brothers and sisters. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those making important decisions: that God may give them wisdom and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those whose families do not understand their faith: that they may keep Christ first with love and patience. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may count the cost of discipleship and follow Jesus with our whole lives. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, who can know your counsel unless you give us wisdom? Send your Holy Spirit, and help us to follow your Son before all else. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Count the cost
reflection.body:
The Book of Wisdom is honest about our limits: "For what man will know the counsel of God?" We hardly understand the things on earth, let alone the things of heaven. The only way to know God's will is if he reveals it: "unless you gave wisdom, and sent your holy spirit from on high." The psalm asks for that wisdom: "So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom."

In the Gospel, great crowds are following Jesus. He turns and speaks to them about what it really means to follow him. His words are strong: anyone who does not put him before father, mother, wife, children, brothers and sisters, and even their own life, "can't be my disciple." Jesus is not telling us to stop loving our families. He is saying that nothing and no one can come before him. In fact, when Christ comes first, we love others better.

Then he gives two images. Someone who wants to build a tower first sits down and counts the cost, so as not to be left with an unfinished building. A king going to war first considers whether he can win. Following Jesus is a decision that must be made seriously. "Whoever doesn't bear his own cross and come after me, can't be my disciple."

The second reading shows the Gospel changing real relationships. Paul sends the runaway slave Onesimus back to his master Philemon, but asks him to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother." In Christ, the old divisions begin to fall.

This week, sit down and count the cost. What is Jesus asking of you that you have been avoiding? Ask the Holy Spirit for wisdom, and take one step of wholehearted discipleship.
